headline: Malaysia names Mossad suspects, but no court has convicted one of spying
context: Since 2018, an assassination, an abduction and an armed Israeli's arrest have been linked by officials to foreign intelligence. Every conviction so far is for guns or abduction, not espionage.

changes.summary: Correction: Earlier editions overstated the role of a Malaysian jailed in the 2024 gun case and what the home minister told Parliament about a private investigator. The man was convicted of consorting with the Israeli; the investigator is accused of being a Mossad informant and is still on trial. The 2025 convictions over the 2022 abduction are now described as abduction, not kidnapping.

cards.big: Suspected Israeli operations in Malaysia share a signature: the operative enters on another country's passport.
cards.sub: The 2018 assassins of a Palestinian lecturer used Serbian and Montenegrin papers; the 2024 gunman flew in French. Dubai's 2010 hit squad did the same.

cards.big: Fadi al-Batsh, a lecturer, was shot about 14 times walking to dawn prayers in Kuala Lumpur.
cards.sub: His killers entered on fake Serbia and Montenegro passports and slipped into Thailand after the April 2018 hit. No one has been charged in Malaysia; the deputy PM cited links to a foreign intelligence agency.

cards.big: In 2022, Malaysians abducted a Gaza programmer in Kuala Lumpur. Prosecutors say they wanted secrets on phone-hacking software.
cards.sub: Six admitted abduction and got five years in 2025. The home minister told Parliament of a private investigator arrested as an alleged Mossad informant. She is still on trial.

cards.big: Every conviction so far is for guns or abduction, never spying.
cards.sub: Seven years for the Israeli, ten and six strokes for a Malaysian who admitted consorting with him, five each for six abductors. Yet about 50 immigration officers were arrested in 2024 for selling foreigners passage.

cards.big: The danger never lay in a hidden cell. It lies in a border for sale and locals hired at arm's length.
Think of a burglar who never picks a lock.
cards.sub: He pays the doorman, hires local hands who never see his face, and leaves on a passport borrowed from a tourist. The police report says trespassing, not burglary.

cards.big: Ministers now name suspects in Parliament, yet the cheapest way in, a bought border and deniable hands, stays open. Suspicion is loud; proof, by design, stays quiet.
